en.title: Videha in Vedic and Upanishadic textual worlds
en.summary: Chapter 5 rests principally on two related but differently transmitted Vedic corpora: the Satapatha Brahmana of the White Yajurveda and the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad that forms the concluding portion of the Satapatha in both its Madhyandina and Kanva recensions. Julius Eggeling's nineteenth-century translation follows the Madhyandina school.

mai.title: वैदिक आ उपनिषदिक पाठ-जगतमे विदेह
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “वैदिक आ उपनिषदिक पाठ-जगतमे विदेह” विषयक प्राचीन विदेह-वज्जि-अंगक पाठ, राजनीतिक संरचना, धर्म आ अभिलेखीय साक्ष्यक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Sources, recensions, and the limits of a textual chronology
Videgha Mathava and the east
Reading Satapatha Brahmana 1.4.1 as a ritual-political narrative
Fire, land, and the danger of a literal clearance model

en.title: Janaka, Sita, and the discipline of reading tradition
en.summary: The Ramayana associates Sita with Janaka and Mithila, and Janakpur became a major centre of pilgrimage and regional identity. The epic is indispensable for the history of ideas, devotion, performance, art, and sacred geography. It is not, by itself, contemporary proof for the reign dates, administrative institutions, or precise borders of an early kingdom.

mai.title: जनक, सीता आ परम्परा पढ़बाक अनुशासन
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “जनक, सीता आ परम्परा पढ़बाक अनुशासन” विषयक प्राचीन विदेह-वज्जि-अंगक पाठ, राजनीतिक संरचना, धर्म आ अभिलेखीय साक्ष्यक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Epic geography and living memory
Multiple textual lives
Why the distinction matters
Epic time and historical time

en.title: Vajji, the Licchavis, and Vaishali
en.summary: The Vajjis enter early Buddhist political narrative as a powerful corporate formation north of the Ganga, with the Licchavis of Vesali or Vaishali among its most visible constituents. Digha Nikaya 16 does not describe a territorial state in modern administrative terms. Instead it presents a political collective whose resilience depends on repeated meetings, concord, inherited rules, respect for elders, limits on coercion against women, maintenance of shrines, and protection of accomplished renunciants.

mai.title: वज्जि, लिच्छवि आ वैशाली
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “वज्जि, लिच्छवि आ वैशाली” विषयक प्राचीन विदेह-वज्जि-अंगक पाठ, राजनीतिक संरचना, धर्म आ अभिलेखीय साक्ष्यक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: A confederated political field
The archive and its asymmetries
Vajji, Licchavi, Videha: names and constituencies
Mishra's 1962 critique of the eight-clan formula

en.title: Anga, Champa, and the Magadhan horizon
en.summary: Anga is one of the clearest examples of why political geography must be reconstructed from several different kinds of evidence. Buddhist lists place Anga among the major polities of northern India, usually beside Magadha; Jain texts also preserve Anga within an eastern political and religious horizon.

mai.title: अंग, चम्पा आ मगधक क्षितिज
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “अंग, चम्पा आ मगधक क्षितिज” विषयक प्राचीन विदेह-वज्जि-अंगक पाठ, राजनीतिक संरचना, धर्म आ अभिलेखीय साक्ष्यक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Anga as a historical problem
Mahajanapada lists and political scale
Early Brahmanical references and the danger of ethnic reading
Epic Anga and Karna: tradition rather than regnal history

en.title: Buddhism, Jainism, and eastern Gangetic religious change
en.summary: The eastern Gangetic plain was not the birthplace of one undifferentiated 'heterodox' movement. Buddhist, Jain, Ajivika, Brahmanical, and other renunciant or ritual communities shared roads, cities, courts, markets, languages, and arguments while maintaining distinct disciplines and claims to authority. Vaishali, Rajagriha, Champa, Mithila, and the wider Magadhan sphere appear repeatedly because political power, urban concentration, merchant wealth, and itinerant teaching converged there.

mai.title: बौद्ध, जैन आ पूर्वी गंगा-मैदानक धार्मिक परिवर्तन
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “बौद्ध, जैन आ पूर्वी गंगा-मैदानक धार्मिक परिवर्तन” विषयक प्राचीन विदेह-वज्जि-अंगक पाठ, राजनीतिक संरचना, धर्म आ अभिलेखीय साक्ष्यक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Shared landscape, distinct traditions
Chronology: founders, texts, and transmitted memory
The sramana field without a single origin story
Greater Magadha as a model, not a map

en.title: Empires, inscriptions, and pilgrim itineraries
en.summary: The appearance of the Mauryas, Guptas, and later supra-regional powers changes the scale at which the history of Mithila, Vajji, Anga, and the Nepal-facing corridor must be written. Empire did not erase local institutions or turn every settlement into an equally administered unit. Royal inscriptions, coins, pillars, seals, roads, tax relations, ritual patronage, and military claims each register different degrees of incorporation.

mai.title: साम्राज्य, अभिलेख आ तीर्थयात्रीक यात्रा-वृत्त
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “साम्राज्य, अभिलेख आ तीर्थयात्रीक यात्रा-वृत्त” विषयक प्राचीन विदेह-वज्जि-अंगक पाठ, राजनीतिक संरचना, धर्म आ अभिलेखीय साक्ष्यक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Empire as a claim with uneven reach
Mauryan north Bihar: monument and text must be separated
Stone, quarry, transport, and state capacity
The first six Pillar Edicts in the Champaran corridor

en.title: Licchavi Nepal and the problem of continuity
en.summary: For this chapter, “Licchavi Nepal” is first of all an inscriptional historical category. The securely dated record in the Kathmandu Valley begins with Mānadeva’s Changu Narayan pillar inscription, whose saṃvat 386 is conventionally converted to 464 CE. From the fifth century onward a substantial Sanskrit epigraphic corpus names rulers, relatives, officials, settlements, taxes, land, religious beneficiaries and acts of donation.
